zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check after scan reading: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510; developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). The index is an aid, not the authority for this copy's typography or wording.

runs.text: Empola que nace nas mãos de traba-

lines.note: Mame is a blister, distinct from the bean entry at the end of f303. The definition begins with blisters on working hands; nace nas is visibly two words, and the headword is flush with the entry margin.

runs.text: lho, ou nos pès de andar. Vt,

lines.note: Lho completes trabalho. Blisters on the feet from walking supply the second location; Mamega starts the Japanese example about a blister developing.

runs.text: Fez ſe me hũa empola nas mãos.

lines.note: Deqita completes mame ga dekita, a blister has formed. The Portuguese makes the first-person hand example explicit and retains the printed nasal signs in hũa and mãos.

runs.text: Hũa certa iguaria feita cõ graõs

lines.note: Mameame names a food made with Japanese beans and a sweet ingredient. This is an independent, unindented headword rather than a continuation of the blister entry.
De Iapão completes the description of the beans. Certo doce adds an unspecified sweet ingredient; no more precise recipe is supplied by the source.

Mamegara denotes bean husks. Although Portuguese casca is expected, enlargement shows an e-like enclosed upper loop in Caſea, agreeing with the aligned OCR. The apparent printed anomaly is retained rather than corrected from meaning alone.
Mamena describes someone diligent and steadfast in work. The new headword is aligned with the left entry margin, not indented as in the provisional draft.
Lho completes trabalho, followed by &c. This short continuation finishes the description of diligence and is correctly indented relative to the headword.
Mameni is the adverb diligently. The italic grammatical label reads Adu., not OCR Ada.; the headword belongs at the entry margin.

Mamenoco is bean flour or meal. The first internal m has lost much of its left side; the nearby Mameni shows similar damage. Mamenoco is the chosen reconstruction, but that consonant remains uncertain rather than fully legible. The supplied NINJAL index independently supports the chosen headword.

runs.text: moidos, que ſeruem pera compoſição doutras

lines.note: The beans are pounded and ground for use in other preparations. Compoſição has long ſ, not f, and doutras contains the t lost by OCR; neither spelling is modernized.
Iguarias completes the reference to other dishes. This is a short continuation of the bean-flour definition, not an omitted or separate entry.

Mameri, mameru, mametta describes becoming soaked or coated, including being covered with flour. The printed principal parts are retained even though they differ from a familiar modern Japanese formulation.

runs.text: nharſe como Mochis em farinha de castanhas

lines.note: Nharſe completes enfarinharſe, being coated in flour, illustrated by Mochis in chestnut flour. Mochis is a Japanese-derived food-name within the Portuguese explanation, visibly italic here.
Doroni mameru means becoming covered with mud. The Portuguese Enlodarſe gives the corresponding muddy or besmeared sense after the preceding flour example.

runs.text: ou enlamearſe. No Cami ſe diz Mabururu.

lines.note: Enlamearſe restates becoming muddy. The Portuguese then identifies Mabururu as the Cami regional form; both Cami and the cited verb occur within that explanatory sentence.
Mamet describes writing being rubbed out or effaced. The historical final t is retained; the following example concerns letters that cannot be read.
Ji ga mamet shite yomenu means the writing is worn away and unreadable. Initial Ii represents ji; the Portuguese has abbreviated Estãdo with a tilde, not the OCR's unmarked Estado.

runs.text: apagada, ou mal aſſentada não ſe lè.

lines.note: The writing cannot be read when effaced or badly set down. The gloss describes the condition of the letters, and the printed aſſentada and lè are preserved.
Mame-otoko is a sincere or upright man. P. marks poetic usage; the Portuguese recto, rather than OCR resto, supplies upright or honest alongside ſimples.
Mamexi is to coat with flour, with Mochis as the object of comparison. The Japanese-derived food-name is embedded in the Portuguese sentence; fa- continues as farinha.

Rinha completes farinha, specifying chestnut and bean flour. Mames is a Japanese-derived bean-name in the Portuguese explanation; abbreviated Itẽ introduces the further muddy-coating sense on the next row.

runs.text: Enlodar, ou encher de lama. No Camiſe diz

lines.note: The additional sense is covering something in mud. The Portuguese begins a regional usage note naming Cami; its tight Camiſe spacing is retained from the scan-aligned draft.

Mabuxi, ſu supplies the Cami form referred to by ſe diz on the previous row. This is a cited Japanese verb within the Portuguese explanation, printed in italic rather than an independent body headword.
Mameshii describes being diligent, alert, or lively in undertaking something. The Portuguese explanation continues with the object of that diligence on the next row.
Fazer algũa couſa completes the positive description. Mameshuu mo nai hito begins the contrasting example of a person lacking that energy; the attached spacing is retained.

To completes fito. The Portuguese describes a person who is not alert or animated, with the alternative description continuing below; the worn middle of eſperto is read with the preceding intact occurrence.
Froxo gives the alternative lax, slack, or listless description. This one-word continuation belongs to the negative example, not the next adjectival entry.
Mameyakana characterizes a diligent, alert person. The scan has two long-s strokes in Peſſoa, restoring the letter omitted by OCR Peſoa without imposing a different double-s allograph.
Mameyakana fumi is a carefully composed letter. The Portuguese begins describing a letter written diligently and at length, with diligente divided across the rows.
Ligente completes diligente; diffuſamente adds at length or fully. The row is visibly indented continuation text, not a new flush-left entry as in the provisional layout.
Mameyakani means with diligence and care. The Portuguese gloss begins with a visibly lowercase c in cõ; Pala- starts a usage comment completed on the following row.
Ura completes Palaura. The dictionary says this expression is commonly used by women; that is the source's usage label, not a claim about present-day speech.
Mami is an animal-name, compared in the Portuguese to an adibe. The historical comparison is preserved without forcing it into a precise modern species identification.
Mamiye, mamiyuru, mamiyeta means appearing or presenting oneself. The Portuguese offers appear or manifest oneself, with the second verb divided across the rows.
Feſtarſe completes mani-feſtarſe, to show or present oneself. The indented short row is a genuine continuation, not an independent entry.
Mamori, mamoru, mamotta means guarding or protecting. The scan clearly reads Mamori rather than OCR Miumori; Vaga starts the supplication involving the speaker's descendants.
Waga shison no ue wo mamoritamaye asks for protection over one's descendants. The honorific imperative is retained in its printed historical form; Defendei begins the Portuguese request.
The Portuguese addresses a lord and asks him to defend and guard the speaker's descendants. This completes the request begun with Defendei, with the continuation indentation restored.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Eſtar com os olhos fixos em algũa

lines.note: The additional sense is keeping one's eyes fixed on something. This visual-attention meaning is distinct from protection and is illustrated by the following Japanese sentence.
Monouo mamoritçumete iru illustrates keeping one's gaze steadily fixed on something. The damaged opening couſa finishes the preceding gloss; the row is continuation text throughout.

runs.text: Estar com os olhos fitos em algũa couſa.

lines.note: The translation repeats having one's eyes fixed on an object. The scan reads os olhos, not OCR orolhos, and the visible indentation places it under the guarding verb's second sense.
Mamori is the noun guarding, protection, or a guard. The Portuguese begins G, not OCR Q; this short independent entry follows the verb and its examples.
Mamushi is equated with kuchihami and glossed as a viper. The old Portuguese Bibora spelling is retained; Ma- starts the example on the following row.
Muxini completes mamushi ni, followed by the passive cuuaruru: to be bitten by a viper. The historical passive form and the tilde carrier in dalgũa are preserved.
Bibora completes the passive-bite translation. This final one-word continuation is indented and must not be promoted to a new entry.
Man is the number ten thousand. Manni fi- begins an example about whether even one instance exists in ten thousand; its continuation is at the top of column 2.
Completes Manni fi-totçumo arǒca, arumaica: whether there is even one in ten thousand. The cedilla in tç and the final Portuguese a- are visible; OCR lost both the cedilla and the line-end division.

runs.text: ueràhum, ou não auerà. i, Couſa que pola mòr

lines.note: Ueràhum completes auerà hum, there will be one, with the tight printed join retained. The explanatory clause describes something unlikely to occur; mòr begins the expression for the greater part or most cases.
Parte completes pola mòr parte, explaining the ten-thousand expression as something that usually will not occur. The physical continuation is retained separately from the following Mana entry.
Mana is a word for fish, described by the compiler as women's usage. The scan reads molheres rather than OCR malheres, and the independent headword is flush with the entry margin.
Riamente completes ordinariamente. The compiler says speakers commonly use the honorific form Vomana; the comma before that form is visible, and Vomana occurs within the Portuguese usage explanation.

This separate Mana concerns a style of writing, not fish. Its initial M and the d in chamada are visible but lost or misread by OCR; Xin introduces the named writing style, followed by an alternative.

Xôſocu completes the alternative script-name after Xin, l. The first o has an upward circumflex rather than the draft's caron; this occurrence is not automatically assimilated to the spelling in Manacana below.

runs.text: Faxes de que vſão os trinchantes.

lines.note: Manabashi are chopsticks used by carvers or food servers. The gloss reads trinchantes, not OCR trinebantes; Faxes is the Japanese-derived implement-name within the Portuguese explanation.
Manabi, u, ǒda gives learning or imitation. The past-tense vowel bears the small downward-pointing mark; retain the historical conjugation rather than substituting a modern paradigm.
The noun Manabi is glossed by imitation or learning. Iẽno starts the Japanese example continued below; its vowel mark and the italic Vt are retained from the scan.
This completes the Japanese example about learning virtue. The rightmost Portuguese character is a fully formed a, not a hyphen: aprender a continues with virtude on the next row.
Virtude completes aprender a virtude. This is a short indented continuation, not a new entry, and its final period is visible.
Manabigaterani expresses doing something in order to learn. The Portuguese prints aprẽder with a nasal abbreviation; do not expand that abbreviation in the canonical line.
Manaca is defined as half a tatami. Tatami is an italic Japanese noun embedded in the Portuguese definition, rather than an independent Japanese example.

The entry names writing styles. The mark after chamada is a comma, and the roman name Xôſô- visibly has the two vowel marks retained here; its unusual printed form is not normalized to the earlier Xôſocu.
Cu completes the broken script name from the previous row. Cana is the name of another script within the Portuguese explanation; the comma after chamão replaces an OCR period.
Manaco is glossed as eyes. A pilcrow introduces Gacumonni manaco, which belongs to the example continued on the following row, not a separate headword.

runs.text: Estar ſempre ſobre o liuro eſtu-

lines.note: Uo ſaraſu completes the Japanese expression for applying the eyes to study. The Portuguese describes constant study over a book; retain its visible eſtu- line break and the baseline st class in Estar.
Dando completes eſtu-dando before the next pilcrow. Manacouo iruru receives the Portuguese senses of attending or applying diligence; both phrases share this physical row.
The first phrase completes the preceding gloss. Manacono tama is followed by the italic editorial preference Meliùs, introducing the better expression on the next row.
Meno tama is the preferred Japanese expression; Bugalho do olho identifies the eyeball. The capital B is weak but has the printed two-bowl form, not a new Japanese initial.

runs.text: Certo aſpecto, ou modo de olhar.

lines.note: Manacozaxi denotes an aspect or manner of looking. Preserve the historical aſpecto spelling and the connected printed ct form rather than reading it as a different word.
The example describes a truly resolved look. Macotoni and vomoiqiritaru remain in roman Japanese example type; no individual words of this standalone example are marked for font toggling.

runs.text: O aſpecto, & modo de olhar era de homem q̃

lines.note: The translation describes the appearance and gaze of a man. The final q̃ is the printed abbreviation for que and continues syntactically with the next row.
The man was resolved to die. The vowel after l is visibly u, correcting reſolito to reſoluto; keep the original lowercase start and provisional st classification in estaua.
Managatçuuo is identified by the historical Portuguese fish name pampano. The cedilla belongs to the Japanese spelling; no modern species name is substituted for the printed gloss.
Manago denotes fine sand. The Portuguese visibly reads Area miuda, with historical Area rather than modern areia and without supplying modern accent marks.
The gloss concerns moving the eyes. The middle letter in menear has an e cross-stroke, correcting OCR mencar; Mana- begins the Japanese example carried onto the next row.
Jiriuo meguraſu completes the example about directing the eyes. Por os olhos, ou olhar begins its Portuguese rendering; the line remains an indented continuation of Manajiri.
The phrase completes the direction of the gaze toward some place. The isolated final S. is retained as printed, rather than expanded speculatively into a citation title.

runs.text: Taboa em que cortão, ou trinchão

lines.note: Manaita is the kitchen board used for cutting or carving. The clause continues below; cortão and trinchão preserve the historical nasal endings visible here.
Na cozinha completes the definition of the cutting board. The scan shows continuation indentation, which is restored instead of treating this short Portuguese row as flush-left entry text.
Manazzuru is glossed as a crane. The doubled zz and the short Portuguese Grou are both visible and need no modernization.
Manben means equality or evenness. The example repeats Manbenni with an initial M, not OCR Nanbenni, and xe- is a real break before the imperative ending below.
Yo completes xeyo, with cubare as an alternative command. Repartiigualmente is tightly set as in the baseline; the row is visibly indented and means to distribute equally.
Manbet is paraphrased as Manni vacaruru and glossed as varying in a thousand ways. The Japanese paraphrase is not an embedded Portuguese term and is left out of typeface_terms.
Maneiras completes the Portuguese definition, then Vt introduces the example about human desire. The printed continuation indentation is restored; xenxa remains the historical Japanese spelling.

runs.text: O deſejo do homẽ de mil ma-

lines.note: Manbet nari completes the Japanese example. The Portuguese translates the changing desires of humankind, with homẽ abbreviated and ma- continuing the word on the next row.
Neiras completes ma-neiras and the clause says that desire changes. This is a short indented continuation, not an independent entry; the long ſ in ſe is retained.
Manbiǒ is paraphrased by Yorozzuno yamai, all illnesses. The gloss breaks do-enças across rows; the small headword vowel mark is retained without normalizing the historical romanization.
Enças completes doenças. The entire short row is Portuguese italic and indented in the scan, so its missing continuation modifier is restored.
Manbiǒyen names a remedy said to work for every illness. The verb is ſerue, with long s rather than the OCR f; the definition itself continues into a qualifying clause below.
The dictionary qualifies the universal-remedy claim with como falão algũs, as some say. Preserve falão and its printed mark; restore the visible indentation of this continuing gloss.
This Manbô denotes all treasures or riches. The Japanese paraphrase contains Yorozzuno, and the Portuguese visibly begins ri- rather than OCR ni-; the headword mark is a circumflex.
Quezas completes riquezas in the preceding gloss. The short row is indented and entirely Portuguese italic; no extra entry or furniture is present.

This separate Manbô entry concerns all laws or teachings. The native crop reads Yorozzuno nori and Todas as leis, ou, repairing the badly corrupted OCR; the printed headword mark points upward, so ô is retained.
Seitas completes the alternative sense of laws or sects. This is the final indented body row; the lower catchword is separate furniture, not part of this gloss.
